Let us begin with the theoretical foundation. Routine Activity Theory, or RAT, begins with a 1979 paper by Lawrence Cohen and Marcus Felson.

After World War II, America faced a paradox. The economy grew, employment rates rose, welfare expanded. Yet crime increased.

Traditional theories that linked crime to poverty and social disadvantage could not explain this paradox.

Cohen and Felson found the cause of this phenomenon in changes in routine activities. As more women entered the workforce, homes were left empty during the day.

At the same time, lightweight, high-value consumer goods became widespread. Things like televisions and portable radios.

From this, they identified three minimal elements of direct-contact predatory violations. First, a motivated offender — someone with both criminal inclinations and the ability to carry them out. Second, a suitable target — a person or object reflecting value, visibility, access, and inertia. Third, the absence of capable guardians — guardians here refer to ordinary citizens who serve to discourage crime in the course of their routine activities.

Cohen and Felson argued that crime occurs when all three elements converge in space and time, and that the lack of any one of them is sufficient to prevent crime.

One point worth noting here is that this framework does not explain how or why the offender becomes motivated in the first place. As the authors stated, they took criminal inclination as given.

Then how do we evaluate whether a target is suitable? On this point, Cohen and Felson described target suitability in terms of four dimensions: Value, Inertia, Visibility, and Access. This is known as the VIVA criteria.

Let us consider an example. A phone left on a cafe table. By VIVA standards, it is a near-perfect target. High value, low inertia, highly visible, and easily accessible.

Let us now see how the original RAT framework was extended. In 2003, John Eck extended the three-element framework into the Crime Triangle. Notice that in Eck's model, the inner triangle consists of offender, target, and place — with place replacing the absence of a capable guardian. Instead, the guardian now appears in the outer triangle as one of three controllers.

These three controllers form the outer triangle. Let us look at the Crime Triangle diagram. The handler is someone who knows the offender well and is in a position to exert control. The guardian refers to ordinary citizens who, going about their routine activities, protect the target. The manager is the owner or designee who has responsibility for controlling behavior at the place.

If any one of these controllers functions properly, crime is likely to be prevented.

Because students often confuse the original model with the extended one, let us compare them at a glance through an actual exam question. On the left is the original RAT framework proposed by Cohen and Felson. On the right is Eck's Crime Triangle, where the concept of controllers is added and an inner-outer dual structure is formed. As we have seen together, understanding how these elements are structured, and what changed in the extended model, is essential.

With the theoretical foundation in place, let us move on to practice. Situational Crime Prevention, first proposed by Clarke in 1992, was later organized by Cornish and Clarke in 2003 around five principles: increasing effort, increasing risk, reducing rewards, reducing provocations, and removing excuses. Each principle contains five specific techniques, 25 in total.

CPTED, or Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, was first proposed by Jeffery and Newman in the early 1970s. It applies these ideas to physical space through strategies such as natural surveillance, access control, and territorial reinforcement. Since then, CPTED has evolved into second and third generation models.

Now, let us apply the situational approach to a specific crime type. Intimate Partner Violence, or IPV, is defined by the CDC as abuse or aggression by a current or former partner. We examine IPV here because it illustrates both the strengths and the limitations of the situational approach.

In 1997, Mannon applied Routine Activity Theory to IPV, and subsequent studies have further explored this connection. In IPV, the offender is often motivated by power, control, or jealousy. The victim is repeatedly exposed in shared living space. And the private nature of the intimate relationship makes guardian intervention structurally difficult.

That said, there is a fundamental limitation of the situational approach when applied to IPV. As long as the relationship continues, the opportunity structure is continuously recreated. Therefore, the situational approach alone cannot fully address violence in this context.

Furthermore, a practical challenge has emerged in recent years. Woodlock, in 2017, found that technology creates what she called perpetrator omnipresence — constant monitoring and control without physical presence. Because the situational approach was designed for physical environments, its application to abuse in digital spaces remains limited.

Today, we have examined the situational approach to crime prevention, from its theoretical foundations to its practical application. To summarize.
투데이 (tʊˈdeɪ), 위 (wiː) 해브 (hæv) 이그재민드 (ɪɡˈzæmɪnd) 더 (ðə) 시추에이셔널 (ˌsɪtʃuˈeɪʃənl) 어프로치 (əˈproʊtʃ) 투 (tuː) 크라임 (kraɪm) 프리벤션 (prɪˈvɛnʃən), 프롬 (frɑːm) 이츠 (ɪts) 씨어레티컬 (ˌθɪəˈrɛtɪkl) 파운데이션즈 (faʊnˈdeɪʃənz) 투 (tuː) 이츠 (ɪts) 프랙티컬 (ˈpræktɪkl) 애플리케이션 (ˌæplɪˈkeɪʃən). 투 (tuː) 서머라이즈 (ˈsʌməˌraɪz)
The situational approach targets opportunity structure. Its theoretical foundation includes Routine Activity Theory, the VIVA criteria, and the Crime Triangle, which lead to practical strategies: SCP and CPTED, and its application to IPV.
더 (ðə) 시추에이셔널 (ˌsɪtʃuˈeɪʃənl) 어프로치 (əˈproʊtʃ) 타겟츠 (ˈtɑːrɡɪts) 아퍼튜니티 (ˌɑːpərˈtuːnɪti) 스트럭처 (ˈstrʌktʃər). 이츠 (ɪts) 씨어레티컬 (ˌθɪəˈrɛtɪkl) 파운데이션 (faʊnˈdeɪʃən) 인클루즈 (ɪnˈkluːdz) — 루틴 (ruːˈtiːn) 액티비티 (ækˈtɪvɪti) 씨어리 (ˈθɪəri), 더 (ðə) 비바 (ˈviːvə) 크라이티리어 (kraɪˈtɪriə), 앤 (ænd) 더 (ðə) 크라임 (kraɪm) 트라이앵글 (ˈtraɪˌæŋɡl) — 위치 (wɪtʃ) 리드 (liːd) 투 (tuː) 프랙티컬 (ˈpræktɪkl) 스트래터지즈 (ˈstrætədʒiz): 에스씨피 (ɛs-siː-piː) 앤 (ænd) 씨피티이디 (siː-piː-tiː-iː-diː), 앤 (ænd) 이츠 (ɪts) 애플리케이션 (ˌæplɪˈkeɪʃən) 투 (tuː) 아이피브이 (aɪ-piː-viː)
Of course, there are limitations. First, this approach is criticized for crime displacement. That means it may relocate crime rather than eliminate it. Second, it takes offender motivation as given. Third, as the IPV case shows, its application to private or digital spaces remains limited.

Despite these limitations, the situational approach remains one of the most practical frameworks in modern criminology. However, as research consistently shows, no single approach is sufficient.
디스파잇 (dɪˈspaɪt) 디즈 (ðiːz) 리미테이션즈 (ˌlɪmɪˈteɪʃənz), 더 (ðə) 시추에이셔널 (ˌsɪtʃuˈeɪʃənl) 어프로치 (əˈproʊtʃ) 리메인즈 (rɪˈmeɪnz) 원 (wʌn) 오브 (ʌv) 더 (ðə) 모스트 (moʊst) 프랙티클 (ˈpræktɪkl) 프레임웍스 (ˈfreɪmˌwɜːrks)
In other words, crime prevention requires a comprehensive understanding based on diverse frameworks and strategies.
